teaching: The prayer from inside the fish is stitched together almost entirely from lines in the Psalms, which is what a person under pressure often prays: borrowed words. It is a thanksgiving for rescue offered before the rescue is complete, from a man who is still swallowed.
It ends with the line the book will test: salvation belongs to the LORD. Jonah says it in the dark and will spend chapter 4 objecting to what it means when it is applied to people he does not like.

lessons.title: The Shortest Sermon
lessons.subtitle: Jonah 3
teaching: Jonah's message is eight words in Hebrew and contains no mention of God, no call to repent and no offer of mercy: forty days and Nineveh will be overthrown. It is the least promising sermon in scripture, and the entire city responds, from the king to the livestock.

The king's decree includes a sentence that is theologically careful — who knows, God may turn and relent — which claims nothing and hopes anyway. The text says God saw their works, that they turned from their evil way, and relented.

lessons.title: Angry Enough to Die
lessons.subtitle: Jonah 4
teaching: The last chapter finally explains the running. Jonah tells God that this is exactly what he expected — that God is gracious and merciful, slow to anger and abundant in loving kindness — and that this is why he fled. He is quoting Exodus 34 back at God as a complaint.

The book ends on a question rather than a resolution. A plant grows, a worm kills it, Jonah is angrier about the plant than about a hundred and twenty thousand people, and God asks whether he should not have pity on a city that cannot tell its right hand from its left. Nobody answers, and the reader is left holding it.

courses.title: Matthew: The Sermon on the Mount
courses.blurb: Three chapters of teaching that have unsettled every generation that has taken them literally.

lessons.title: Blessed Are
lessons.subtitle: Matthew 5:1–16
teaching: The Beatitudes are announcements rather than instructions. Nobody is told to become poor in spirit or to mourn; the sentences declare that people already in those conditions are the fortunate ones, which inverts every list of the blessed the audience would have known.

The images that follow — salt that has lost its taste, a city on a hill, a lamp under a basket — are all about being unavoidably noticeable. The sermon opens by telling people with no status that they are the point, and then that they cannot be hidden.

lessons.title: You Have Heard It Said
lessons.subtitle: Matthew 5:17–48
teaching: Six times Jesus quotes a command and then goes behind it to the disposition underneath: murder to contempt, adultery to the appetite, oaths to plain speech, retaliation to non-resistance. The pattern is not the loosening of the law that his critics expected but a tightening of it.

The section on enemies is the hardest and is stated without qualification: love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you, because God sends rain on the just and the unjust alike. Christians have differed for centuries over how far this extends into public and political life, and the disagreement is not a modern invention.

lessons.title: In Secret
lessons.subtitle: Matthew 6:1–18
teaching: The three practices addressed — giving, praying, fasting — were the pillars of devout life, and the instruction for each is identical in shape: do it, and do it where nobody can see. The warning is not against the practices but against performing them.

The Lord's Prayer sits in the middle of this and is notably short. It asks for bread for today rather than security, and ties being forgiven to forgiving, which is the one clause the passage circles back to afterwards to underline.

lessons.title: Do Not Be Anxious
lessons.subtitle: Matthew 6:19–34
teaching: The argument moves from treasure to sight to service and lands on a claim rather than a comfort: you cannot serve God and money. The word used for money is mammon, and treating it as a rival master rather than a neutral tool is the section's whole move.

What follows is not advice to stop caring. It is an argument from observation — birds, lilies, the shortness of a life you cannot extend by worrying — ending in an instruction about sequence: seek first the kingdom, and let tomorrow carry its own trouble.

lessons.title: Ask, and Judge Not
lessons.subtitle: Matthew 7:1–14
teaching: The instruction about judging is regularly quoted as a ban on all moral assessment, which the same paragraph rules out by telling the reader to remove the plank and then help with the speck. The target is the disqualifying inconsistency, not the helping.

The section on asking uses ordinary parental logic — you would not hand your child a stone instead of bread — and the golden rule arrives as the summary of the law and the prophets. The gate that follows is narrow, and Matthew does not soften it.

lessons.title: Two Foundations
lessons.subtitle: Matthew 7:15–29
teaching: The sermon ends with tests rather than summaries: fruit rather than claims, doing rather than saying. The most sobering paragraph is addressed to people who prophesied and performed miracles and are told they were never known, which places the sermon's warning inside the religious community rather than outside it.

The closing image gives both houses the same storm. The difference is not the weather but the foundation, and the foundation is defined as hearing these words and doing them. Matthew notes that the crowds were astonished, because he taught as one having authority rather than as their scribes.

courses.title: 1 Corinthians: A Difficult Church
courses.blurb: Factions, lawsuits, a chaotic communion table and a famous chapter on love — written to a congregation in trouble.

lessons.title: I Follow Paul, I Follow Apollos
lessons.subtitle: 1 Corinthians 1
teaching: Corinth was a wealthy port city with a mixed population and a reputation, and the church there had split into parties named after their favourite teachers. Paul's first move is to point out that none of them was crucified for anyone, and that he can barely remember whom he baptised.

The argument goes to the message itself: a crucified messiah was an offence to Jews expecting deliverance and nonsense to Greeks trained in rhetoric. Paul does not soften it. He says God chose what the world calls foolish and weak, and points out that not many of them were influential to begin with.

lessons.title: A Table That Divides
lessons.subtitle: 1 Corinthians 11
teaching: The problem at the communion meal is social before it is theological. The wealthier members, whose time was their own, arrived early and ate; those who worked arrived to nothing. Paul says that meeting like this means it is not the Lord's supper they are eating at all.

The words of institution he quotes are the earliest written record of them, predating the Gospels. What is striking is the context he puts them in: the remedy for eating unworthily is not more introspection but waiting for one another. The doctrine is deployed to fix a seating problem.

lessons.title: One Body, Many Parts
lessons.subtitle: 1 Corinthians 12
teaching: The body image was a standard piece of Greco-Roman political rhetoric, normally used to tell the lower orders to stay in their place. Paul takes the familiar figure and turns it: the parts that seem weaker are indispensable, and the less honourable are given greater honour.

The list of gifts is deliberately varied and deliberately unranked in worth, though Paul does order them by usefulness to others. The chapter's conclusion is that a body cannot be composed of one organ, which is aimed squarely at a congregation prizing one spectacular gift above the rest.

lessons.title: The More Excellent Way
lessons.subtitle: 1 Corinthians 13
teaching: The love chapter is read at weddings and was written into an argument about spiritual one-upmanship. Its first move is to price the gifts the Corinthians were competing over — tongues, prophecy, knowledge, faith, even martyrdom — at nothing without love.

The description that follows is almost entirely made of verbs and negatives: patient, kind, does not envy, does not boast, is not puffed up, does not seek its own, is not provoked, keeps no record of wrongs. It is a list of behaviours rather than feelings, which is what makes it usable.

lessons.title: If Christ Has Not Been Raised
lessons.subtitle: 1 Corinthians 15
teaching: Paul hands on a summary he says he received — died, was buried, was raised, appeared — and then lists witnesses including more than five hundred at once, most of whom he notes are still alive, which is an invitation to check.

The argument he builds is unusually blunt for a religious text: if the resurrection did not happen, the preaching is empty, the faith is futile, and the apostles are liars. He does not offer the doctrine as a helpful metaphor. The chapter ends in practical terms — be steadfast, immovable, because the labour is not in vain.

courses.title: Ephesians: Grace and the New Humanity
courses.blurb: Three chapters of what is true, three of what to do about it — and a wall pulled down in the middle.

lessons.title: Every Spiritual Blessing
lessons.subtitle: Ephesians 1
teaching: The opening of Ephesians is one enormous sentence in Greek, and its breathlessness is part of the point: chosen, adopted, redeemed, forgiven, sealed. Nothing in the list is something the reader did, and the paragraph keeps returning to the phrase 'to the praise of his glory'.

The prayer that closes the chapter asks not for new circumstances but for sight — that the eyes of their hearts would be enlightened to know what they already have. Christians differ sharply over the chapter's language of choosing, and those differences are serious and old; the passage's own emphasis falls on what the choosing is for.

lessons.title: By Grace, Through Faith
lessons.subtitle: Ephesians 2:1–10
teaching: The paragraph begins with a diagnosis stated in the past tense — dead in trespasses, following the course of this world — and then interrupts itself with two words that carry the whole letter: but God. The sentence structure enacts the argument.

Then the summary: by grace you have been saved through faith, and that not of yourselves, it is the gift of God, not of works, so that no one can boast. And immediately after, the balance most quoting of the passage omits — we are his workmanship, created for good works prepared beforehand. Works are the destination, not the entry fee.

lessons.title: The Wall Pulled Down
lessons.subtitle: Ephesians 2:11–22
teaching: The dividing wall Paul refers to was probably literal: the barrier in the Jerusalem temple beyond which Gentiles could not pass on pain of death. Its inscription has been found. He says it has been abolished, and that the two groups are made into one new humanity.

The images pile up — no longer strangers and foreigners but fellow citizens, members of the household, a building fitted together into a temple. For a first-century reader the claim that Jew and Gentile now share one household was not a sentiment but a social earthquake.

lessons.title: Walk Worthy
lessons.subtitle: Ephesians 4
teaching: Chapter 4 is where the letter turns from indicative to imperative, and the first instruction is about how to treat each other: humility, gentleness, patience, bearing with one another in love, eager to maintain unity. Unity is presented as something to be kept rather than created.

The practical list that follows is startlingly concrete — tell the truth, do not let the sun go down on your anger, stop stealing and work so you have something to give away, let no corrupting talk come out of your mouth. It ends with kindness and forgiveness modelled on having been forgiven.

courses.title: Philippians: Joy from a Prison Cell
courses.blurb: The most cheerful letter in the New Testament, written by a man in chains to a church he loved.

lessons.title: To Live Is Christ
lessons.subtitle: Philippians 1
teaching: Paul is under guard and possibly facing execution, and his report on the situation is that it has actually advanced the message — the whole praetorian guard has heard why he is there. He even notes that some are preaching out of rivalry to make his imprisonment harder, and says he does not care as long as the message goes out.

The sentence the chapter is known for is a genuine dilemma rather than a slogan: for me to live is Christ and to die is gain. He works through both sides honestly, concludes that staying is more useful to them, and settles it there.

lessons.title: The Mind of Christ
lessons.subtitle: Philippians 2
teaching: The hymn in chapter 2 is widely thought to predate the letter, quoted rather than composed here. It traces a descent — equality with God not clung to, emptied, taking the form of a servant, obedient to death, even death on a cross — and then a reversal, exalted and given the name above every name.

Its framing is the surprise. Paul introduces this soaring passage as an argument for a practical instruction: do nothing from selfish ambition, count others better than yourselves, look to their interests. The highest thing the letter says about Christ is deployed to settle a disagreement between two women in the congregation.

lessons.title: Counting It Loss
lessons.subtitle: Philippians 3
teaching: Paul lists his credentials — circumcised the eighth day, of the tribe of Benjamin, a Pharisee, blameless under the law — and then writes them all off, using a word most translations soften considerably. The point is not that they were bad but that he no longer counts them as assets.

What replaces the ledger is a race: forgetting what is behind, straining toward what is ahead, pressing on toward the goal. He is explicit that he has not already obtained it, which is a notable thing for the writer to say about himself.

lessons.title: Learned to Be Content
lessons.subtitle: Philippians 4
teaching: The chapter opens by naming two women in disagreement and asking a third party to help them, which is the most specific pastoral moment in the letter. The famous instruction about anxiety follows immediately: do not be anxious, but in everything by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving, let your requests be made known.

The contentment Paul describes is explicitly a learned skill rather than a temperament — he says he has learned it, in plenty and in hunger. That context is worth keeping attached to the verse about doing all things through him who strengthens, which is otherwise routinely quoted about achievement.

courses.title: Hebrews: Better Things
courses.blurb: A sermon to people thinking of giving up, arguing that what they already have is better than what they miss.

lessons.title: God Has Spoken
lessons.subtitle: Hebrews 1
teaching: Hebrews does not open like a letter — no greeting, no named sender — and reads more like a sermon sent in writing. Its first sentence sets the whole argument: God spoke in many portions and many ways through the prophets, and has now spoken in a Son.

The chapter then argues from a chain of Old Testament quotations that the Son is greater than the angels, which seems an odd priority until you notice the audience. These were people tempted to go back to something they regarded as angelically mediated and therefore weighty.

lessons.title: A Sympathetic High Priest
lessons.subtitle: Hebrews 4
teaching: The image of the word of God as living and active, sharper than a two-edged sword, is usually quoted alone. In place it is the conclusion of a warning about a generation that heard a promise and did not enter it, and the point is that nothing about the hearer stays hidden.

What follows immediately is the counterweight, and the two belong together: we do not have a high priest who cannot sympathise with our weaknesses. The invitation is to come boldly — the word carries the sense of speaking freely — to find mercy and grace in time of need.

lessons.title: By Faith
lessons.subtitle: Hebrews 11
teaching: The chapter's definition of faith is about substance and evidence rather than feeling, and what follows is a roll call: Abel, Noah, Abraham, Sarah, Moses, Rahab. It is a list of people who acted on something they could not yet see, and the writer is careful to say they died without receiving what was promised.

The second half of the chapter is the part usually left out of the summary. After the conquests and the stopped mouths of lions come those who were tortured, mocked, imprisoned, sawn in two, and destitute — described in the same breath and with the same commendation. Faith here does not predict the outcome.

lessons.title: Run the Race
lessons.subtitle: Hebrews 12
teaching: The cloud of witnesses in chapter 12 is the crowd of chapter 11, and the image is athletic: lay aside the weight and the entangling sin, and run with endurance the race set before you, looking to Jesus. Endurance rather than speed is the quality named throughout.

The passage on discipline that follows is difficult and has been misused to justify a great deal. Its own claim is narrower than the uses made of it: that hardship endured in this relationship is not evidence of rejection, and that it yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness to those trained by it.

lessons.title: Outside the Camp
lessons.subtitle: Hebrews 13
teaching: The closing chapter turns practical in a list of short instructions: keep loving one another, show hospitality to strangers, remember prisoners as though in prison with them, keep your life free from the love of money, be content with what you have.

The image of going to him outside the camp, bearing his reproach, is addressed to people whose faith had cost them their standing in their own community. The letter ends by telling them that the loss of a permanent city here is not the disaster it appears to be, and that Jesus Christ is the same yesterday, today and forever.

courses.title: James: Faith That Works
courses.blurb: The bluntest book in the New Testament — on the tongue, on money, on favouritism, and on faith you can actually see.

lessons.title: Count It All Joy
lessons.subtitle: James 1
teaching: James opens by telling people to count trials as joy, and the reason given is mechanical rather than sentimental: testing produces endurance, and endurance finishes its work. The letter is full of this kind of plain cause and effect.

The offer of wisdom to anyone who asks sits right next to it, along with a warning about asking while doubting. The chapter closes with the letter's thesis in miniature: be doers of the word and not hearers only, and a definition of pure religion that is entirely about widows, orphans and self-control.

lessons.title: The Seat by the Door
lessons.subtitle: James 2:1–13
teaching: The scenario is specific: a man in fine clothes with a gold ring and a poor man in shabby clothes arrive at the same meeting, and one is offered a good seat while the other is told to stand or sit on the floor. James calls this becoming judges with evil thoughts.

The argument he makes is not that the poor are more deserving but that favouritism contradicts the faith being professed, and he ties it to the law of love and to mercy triumphing over judgement. It is one of the most socially concrete passages in the New Testament.

lessons.title: Faith Without Works
lessons.subtitle: James 2:14–26
teaching: This is the passage Luther struggled with, and the tension with Paul is worth stating rather than smoothing over. James says a person is justified by works and not by faith alone; Paul says by faith apart from works of the law. Both cite Abraham.

The common resolution is that the two are answering different questions — Paul on how a person is accepted, James on how a claimed faith is recognised — and that they use 'works' to mean different things. James's own illustration is unanswerable on its own terms: telling a cold and hungry person to keep warm and well fed while giving them nothing.

lessons.title: A Small Fire
lessons.subtitle: James 3
teaching: James's images for the tongue escalate deliberately: a bit in a horse's mouth, a rudder on a ship, and then a spark that sets a forest alight. The first two are about small things steering large ones; the third is about small things destroying them.

The observation he lands on is the uncomfortable one — that blessing and cursing come out of the same mouth, and that a spring does not produce both fresh and salt water. The chapter ends by contrasting two kinds of wisdom, and the heavenly one is described almost entirely in terms of how it treats other people.

lessons.title: Tomorrow and the Prayer of Faith
lessons.subtitle: James 4–5
teaching: The rebuke of those who say they will go to such a city and trade and make a profit is not against planning but against the certainty — you do not know what tomorrow brings. The correction offered is a phrase, if the Lord wills, meant as a genuine posture rather than a verbal tic.

Chapter 5 opens with the sharpest economic language in the New Testament, addressed to the rich whose withheld wages are crying out. It closes gently, with prayer, anointing, confession to one another, and the note that Elijah was a man with a nature like ours.

courses.title: 1 John: Light, Love and Assurance
courses.blurb: A short letter written to people who had been told they were missing something — on how to know that you are not.

lessons.title: What We Have Seen
lessons.subtitle: 1 John 1
teaching: The opening insists on the physical: what we have heard, what we have seen with our eyes, what we have looked at and our hands have touched. The letter is written against teaching that treated the material world, and a genuinely embodied Christ, as beneath God.

The claim that follows — God is light and in him is no darkness at all — is paired immediately with a practical test about walking in that light, and with an admission the letter keeps making room for: if we say we have no sin we deceive ourselves.

lessons.title: Called Children of God
lessons.subtitle: 1 John 3:1–10
teaching: See what kind of love the Father has given us, that we should be called children of God — and the writer adds, almost as an aside, that this is why the world does not recognise us. Identity and unfamiliarity are treated as the same fact.

What follows is honest about the gap between now and later: we are God's children now, and what we will be has not yet appeared. The passage's strong statements about not continuing in sin have been read in several ways, and the differences turn largely on the tense of the Greek verbs.

lessons.title: Love in Deed and Truth
lessons.subtitle: 1 John 3:11–24
teaching: The letter's definition of love is not a feeling but an act, and it gives both a supreme example and an everyday one in consecutive sentences: he laid down his life for us, and if anyone has the world's goods and sees a brother in need and closes his heart, how does God's love abide in him?

The instruction that follows — let us not love in word or with the tongue only, but in deed and truth — leads into one of the most pastorally useful lines in the New Testament, addressed to people whose own hearts condemn them: God is greater than our heart, and knows all things.

lessons.title: Perfect Love Casts Out Fear
lessons.subtitle: 1 John 4
teaching: The chapter contains the letter's most quoted sentence, God is love, and it is worth reading the sentences on either side of it. Love is defined not as our reaching but as his sending, and the immediate conclusion drawn is an obligation: if God so loved us, we also ought to love one another.

The line about fear is precise. There is no fear in love, because perfect love casts out fear, and fear has to do with punishment. It is written to people who were being made anxious about whether they measured up, and its answer is not to try harder but to look at where the love started.

courses.title: Revelation: Hope Under Pressure
courses.blurb: The most argued-over book in the Bible, read the way its first readers did — as encouragement under an empire.

lessons.title: A Letter, Not a Puzzle
lessons.subtitle: Revelation 1
teaching: Revelation announces itself as three things at once: an apocalypse, a prophecy, and a letter to seven named churches in what is now western Turkey. The last of those is the most often forgotten, and it is the one that governs how the book was first heard.

Reading approaches differ enormously — some place its events in the first century, some at the end of history, some see a symbolic account of the whole church age, some a cyclical retelling. This course does not choose between them. It reads for what the book says to churches under pressure, which every approach agrees is its function.

lessons.title: Letters to Real Churches
lessons.subtitle: Revelation 2–3
teaching: The seven messages follow a pattern — a description of Christ, a commendation, a rebuke, a call, a promise — and their details are local. Laodicea's lukewarm water, Sardis's reputation for being alive, Smyrna's poverty are all things those cities would have recognised about themselves.

Two of the seven receive no rebuke at all, and both are the ones under the most external pressure. The most quoted image in the section, standing at the door and knocking, is addressed to a church, not to an individual outsider — it is Christ asking to be let back into his own congregation.

lessons.title: The Lamb Who Was Slain
lessons.subtitle: Revelation 5
teaching: The turning point of the book's imagery happens in chapter 5. A scroll cannot be opened, and John weeps; he is told to stop because the Lion of the tribe of Judah has conquered. Then he looks, and what he sees standing there is a Lamb, looking as though it had been slain.

The substitution is the interpretive key to everything after it. The victory the book celebrates is repeatedly described in the language of conquest and repeatedly shown in the shape of a sacrifice, and readers who miss that swap tend to misread the rest of the visions badly.

lessons.title: A Crowd Nobody Could Count
lessons.subtitle: Revelation 7
teaching: Between the sixth and seventh seals the narrative pauses, and John hears a number and then sees a crowd — a multitude from every nation, tribe, people and language that no one could count. The pause is placed deliberately at the point of maximum tension.

The description of them is where the chapter's comfort lies: they came out of the great tribulation, and God will wipe away every tear from their eyes. The book is not telling frightened readers that nothing will happen to them; it is telling them what is on the other side of it.

lessons.title: A New Heaven and a New Earth
lessons.subtitle: Revelation 21–22
teaching: The ending is not an evacuation. The city comes down, and the dwelling place of God is with people — the direction of travel is toward the world rather than away from it, which is worth noticing given how often the book is summarised the other way round.

What is promised is stated as removal before it is stated as addition: no more death, mourning, crying or pain, for the former things have passed away. And then the only line in scripture spoken from the throne in the middle of a vision of the end: behold, I am making all things new.
